A.headline: At a hundred, a small island that learned to share its bets
A.dek: Singapore turns one hundred with a Citizens' Assembly, a care guarantee and a water compact it co-owns with Johor.
lead: Singapore turns one hundred tonight the way it has handled most of the last four decades: argue in public, then build. Parliament last week passed the Centenary Compact, a ten-year framework that ties a share of the national reserves' returns to a citizen dividend, a care guarantee for the very old and a standing fund for the sea wall. A Citizens' Assembly of 400 randomly chosen residents spent eight weekends rewriting the first draft.

The compact is the latest step in a quiet re-bargaining. Facing a super-aged citizenry, a workforce in which citizens had become a minority of the working day, and the end of the 1962 Johor water agreement in 2061, the republic chose to widen the table rather than narrow it. Opposition parties hold about a third of elected seats. The government still governs, but it now bargains over budgets.

The world outside stayed open enough to make that affordable. Green-fuel bunkering, regional power trading on the ASEAN grid and a trusted-data and biomedical sector keep the island needed. Nobody here thinks the hub is safe by right. Indispensable, one minister says, is a subscription renewed every year.

street.title: “I tell them what the block needs”
street.text: Rohani binte Ismail, 71, works three mornings a week as a care navigator at the Toa Payoh health hub, walking the lifts and corridors of her old estate to check on neighbours older than she is. She ran a school canteen for thirty years and was a stranger to computers until the retraining credits arrived at 58. The part-pension and part-wage mean she does not have to choose between rest and rent. Her grandson tests ammonia-fuel valves in Tuas. “In my mother's time you waited to be told what you would be,” she says. “Now I tell them what the block needs.” It is hotter than she would like, and the flat's lease has a long tail under the Home Continuity Scheme. But the lift works, the neighbours know her name, and tonight the block will watch the fireworks from the void deck.

side: Johor–Singapore compact enters its fifth year
Sea wall's eastern arc opens to the public
voices: The bank's AI took the routine half of my compliance job and the national credit took me to the other half. I earn less per hour and more per year, and my evenings are my own.
Priya Nair, 44, compliance specialist, Bukit Merah
The rent on my stall is set by a formula the whole street voted on. I do not love the formula. I love that I helped write it.
Mr Chew, 58, coffee-shop owner, Tiong Bahru
I came on a work permit to build the sea wall. Eleven years later my daughter is a citizen. I still send money to Kerala, and I no longer feel like furniture.
Joseph Mathew, 49, site supervisor, permanent resident
A.takeaway: The hub holds because enough citizens still feel it is theirs. The task of the second century is to widen that number before the next shock tests the arithmetic.

full.byline: By our National Affairs Editor · Marina Bay
full.pull: We stopped asking whether the island could be safe and started asking who it is safe for.
full.pullBy: A member of the Citizens' Assembly

side.h: Johor–Singapore compact enters its fifth year
side.p: Joint reservoirs, a shared grid and a water price indexed to rainfall. Both capitals call it boring, which is the highest praise in diplomacy.

side.h: Sea wall's eastern arc opens to the public
side.p: The East Coast polder is a park by day and a flood barrier by night. Phase three begins next year.
Citizens over 70 can draw a part-pension and a part-wage, with employers co-funding redesigned roles.
Solar canopies and misting fans, voted for by the stallholders themselves.

letters: The assembly argued for eight weekends and I still disagree with half of it. That is how I know it was real. — Reader, Clementi
Print this: my dividend paid for my mother's hearing aids. — Reader, Bedok
A hundred years and we are still arguing about the lift upgrade. Long may it last. — Retired civil servant, Hougang
full.commentTitle: A hundred years, and a seat for everyone who pays the bill
full.comment: The republic's centenary is not a story of triumph but of stubborn inclusion. We did not defeat the heat or the sea. We built, late and not always gracefully, the habit of asking before we spend. The hub holds because enough citizens still feel it is theirs. The task of the second century is to widen that number before the next shock tests the arithmetic.
full.extrapolated: A working citizens' assembly, a citizen dividend, a care guarantee, a co-owned water and power compact with Johor, and a more competitive Parliament. Tell us if any of these is a step too far, or not far enough.
questions: What concretely holds a broad compact together once cheap-growth years end? Name the institutions and bargains you find plausible, and say whether they are a departure from today's style of governing or already latent in it.
Is forty years of open world plausible? What keeps the straits open and Singapore indispensable when major powers hedge?
Who loses in this world: landlords, younger citizens paying for the silver generation, non-resident workers? Why do they accept it?
How does the political system change to carry a broad compact? What is the minimum change that counts?
On the street: whose life genuinely improves, and whose merely stabilises?

drift.drifting: Towards the top right if the world fragments and adaptation costs spike. Towards the bottom left if the dividend turns into a payment for silence.
levers: A funded, standing citizens' assembly with binding budget lines
Keeping citizen ownership of homes and wealth growing at least as fast as GDP

B.name: Lifeboat Republic
B.line: The world splits and the island pulls together: a smaller economy and a shared burden.

B.headline: At a hundred, a lifeboat that kept everyone aboard
B.dek: Singapore turns one hundred in a smaller, fairer, more watchful economy, with a ration formula everyone can read.
lead: Singapore turns one hundred in the fifth year of what the government calls the Long Resilience: the deliberate shrinking of the island's exposure to a world divided into trading blocs, sanction regimes and contested sea lanes. Parliament last night extended National Resilience Service to every citizen aged 18 to 65, with medical, logistics, cyber and engineering tracks beside the armed forces, and fixed the ration-share formula for fuel and food for another decade.

The economy is smaller than the forecasts of 2026 promised. Container volumes are down by a third from their peak as supply chains split into regional loops, and finance has fragmented into three clearing systems that the island joins one at a time. What it has instead is cohesion. Housing, health and food costs are shared. Shortages are rationed by published rule, not by price.

The island's wager is neutrality with a purpose: a trusted place for escrow, arbitration, data custody and marine insurance for parties who no longer trust each other. It is a thin living. We are the hospital in the war, one official says, not the arms dealer.

street.title: “We are not asked to be heroes, only to turn up”
street.text: Faridah Yusof, 39, coordinates a community pantry hub a short walk from the Causeway. Four days a month she works Resilience Service shifts; the rest of the time she is a logistics planner at a firm that now ships mostly within Southeast Asia. Her husband is a nurse and her income is lower than her mother's was at her age. She does not romanticise it. The queue for the weekly ration is orderly because everyone knows the formula, and because a retired headmaster audits it on Thursdays. “It is not generous,” she says, “but it is fair, and fair is what we can afford.” Her daughter wants to study marine insurance, a profession that exists mainly because nobody else is trusted. Tonight the family will watch the drone lights from their balcony, eight storeys up, with the fans on.

side: ASEAN-lite food and power pact renewed
voices: My firm used to write policies for forty countries. Now we write for fourteen, and we write them carefully. I earn a third less. My grandchildren will have a smaller career and a fuller table.
Raymond Ong, 61, marine insurer, Telok Blangah
I did my service at eighteen and again at fifty-eight. The second time I taught teenagers to repair a power transformer. Both times I felt useful.
Gurmit Singh, 59, electrician, Yishun
Do not call it sacrifice. Call it the price of a table that is still set for everyone.
Mdm Chan, 72, retired teacher, Queenstown
B.takeaway: A lifeboat works only if nobody is told to swim. The question is whether the burden is shared by rule, or only among citizens.

full.byline: By our Economics Editor · Tanjong Pagar
full.pull: A lifeboat works only if nobody is told to swim.

side.p: Rice, fuel and medical stock now held to a published formula, with a Parliament committee holding the keys.

side.h: ASEAN-lite food and power pact renewed
side.p: Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore share the grid and the harvest. The water compact with Johor holds under the Long Agreement.
Retired technicians run the night shift at the pantry hubs, paid in credits as well as cash.
Drone lights charged from rooftop panels replace the display. We save the watts, said one mayor.

letters: The ration card is the only document I have ever been proud to show. — Reader, Sembawang
Why do foreign workers get a lower ration tier? Fair for whom? — Reader, Geylang
My son did his Resilience Service in cyber. He now thinks he can protect a grid. Good. — Reader, Pasir Ris
full.comment: The nation's second century begins by paying a bill its first deferred. For decades the island treated openness as a law of nature. It was a favour, and the favour has been withdrawn. What remains to be decided is who pays. If the burden is shared by rule, this is a story of solidarity. If it is shared only among citizens, it is a story of a narrower circle, with better manners.
full.extrapolated: A fragmented world, a smaller hub, a fair rationing system, citizen-wide service and a regional neighbours' pact. If you think this world cannot hold and collapses into securitised control, it becomes Garrison City (D). Say so.
questions: Does a fragmented world still leave Singapore a niche worth having (neutral custody, arbitration, insurance), or does hub status erode faster than cohesion can compensate? If the latter, B becomes D.
What do citizens give up (consumption, mobility, voice) to fund resilience, and why do they accept it?
A broad compact for citizens can be a narrow compact for everyone else. What happens to the non-resident workforce when the economy shrinks?
Do Malaysia and Indonesia cooperate or compete over scarce resources? What happens at the Causeway and at the 2061 water deadline?
On the street: is this a story of solidarity or of managed decline?

drift.drifting: Towards the bottom right (D) if shortages turn rationing into a security matter and discretion replaces rule. Towards the top left (A) if the blocs thaw.

C.name: Gilded Hub
C.line: The world still wants the island. The island's people are less sure it still wants them.
signals: Median citizen income versus GDP per head

C.headline: At a hundred, a city the whole world wants, and fewer of its own can afford
C.dek: Record capital and arrivals, a compute campus and a sea wall on time, while citizens become tenants in their own city.
lead: Singapore marks its centenary with record arrivals, record capital inflows and a National Day Parade staged for a global audience in seven languages. The island hosts more than four hundred regional headquarters, and its largest compute campus at Tuas now draws a fifth of the island's power. Officials call the decade a golden compounding.

Beneath the figures sits a quieter story. Citizens are a shrinking minority of the people who live and work here, and a shrinking share of those who run its institutions. Median citizen household income has barely moved in a decade as AI agents absorbed mid-skill white-collar work, while the price of space has outrun every wage. Home is increasingly something rented from the market or held on an expiring lease.

The political arrangement is stable. Elections are held, results are not in doubt, and consultation is thorough, polite and largely non-binding. Officials say a narrow base is the price of speed. Critics say speed is the price of a narrow base. The sea wall, the grid and the new Johor water compact were all delivered on time and on budget. Few were asked.

street.title: “We are the staff of a very successful hotel”
street.place: On the street · Bedok, and Tuas
street.text: Daniel Lim, 38, was an operations analyst at a bank until AI agents absorbed his team. He now drives for a platform and lives with his parents in a four-room flat in Bedok with eighteen years left on the lease. “Singapore is the best place in the world to visit,” he says, without bitterness. “To be a citizen, you start to feel like staff at a very successful hotel.” Fifteen kilometres west, Anjali Rao, 29, an AI safety researcher on a Global Resident pass, runs evaluations at the Tuas campus and loves the city's order, its food and its safety. In a dormitory beyond the fence, Rubel Hossain, 31, sleeps eight to a room in a building with a gym. He has not seen the sea wall, only the road to it. Tonight all three will watch the same fireworks, from three different distances.

side: First lease-end notices posted in Queenstown
Global Resident class tops one million
voices: I have never earned more or had less to say about where I live. Both can be true. I don't complain, I am too busy.
Anjali Rao, 29, AI safety researcher, Global Resident
My father built the flat. My son will be sent a letter about it.
Mr Tan, 64, retired technician, Queenstown
We sleep eight to a room in a dormitory with a gym. I have not seen the sea wall, only the road to it.
Rubel Hossain, 31, construction worker, Tuas
C.takeaway: The city works. The question is for whom it works, and for how long the citizen core will stay content as tenants.

full.byline: By our Business Editor · Raffles Place
full.pull: The city works. The question is for whom it works.
full.pullBy: A former civil servant, on the centenary

side.h: First lease-end notices posted in Queenstown
side.p: Residents of the earliest 99-year flats are offered relocation to rental flats or a cash-out at the residual-value formula.

side.h: Global Resident class tops one million
side.p: A fast-track pass for senior talent. Citizens now hold fewer than four in ten professional posts.
A fifth of the island's power, and a growing share of its political patience.
Grants have moved to partnership programmes. Several advocacy groups have quietly closed.

letters: Investment is up and the streets are safe. What more does a citizen need? — Reader, Orchard
Three letters on lease reversion were received this week. None could be printed. — The Editor
My daughter says her generation will be tourists in their own city. I told her to enjoy the view. — Reader, Marine Parade
full.commentTitle: A hundred years of success, and the guest list
full.comment: The island has done what small places are not supposed to do: remain essential to a bigger world. For that the republic deserves its fireworks. But a centenary is also an occasion to ask who is on the guest list. A state that serves capital and talent faithfully while its own citizens quietly become tenants is not failing. It is succeeding at the wrong thing.
full.extrapolated: An open world, a fast and efficient state, high-quality infrastructure delivered on time, and a citizen core whose median position has stalled. Challenge any of it, especially how consent is kept.
questions: Can an open world and a narrow compact coexist for four decades? What makes citizens consent, or merely comply, when most gains go to mobile capital and talent?
Show us the mechanisms: how is consent manufactured, bought or lost (housing, dividends, security, status)?
Who exactly benefits, and what do citizen elites receive to remain supportive?
Lease decay: what happens to the citizen asset base as the first flats revert? Does this world have a political release valve?
On the street: how does life differ for a Bedok citizen, a Tuas researcher and a dormitory worker? If the open world closes, does C slide into D?

drift.drifting: Towards the bottom right (D) if the world fragments while the compact is already thin. Upwards towards A if citizen ownership and voice are rebuilt while the hub is still strong.

D.name: Garrison City
D.line: The hard case: a secure island, a narrowed public life and a state in permanent management mode.
signals: Emergency renewals becoming routine

D.headline: At a hundred, an island on watch
D.dek: An indoor parade, an Emergency Resource Order in its fourteenth year and care circles filling the gaps the state has squeezed.
lead: Singapore marks one hundred years with a ceremony indoors. The National Day Parade was moved to a roofed arena for the third year running, citing maritime security conditions, and the Government last night extended the Emergency Resource Order for a further twelve months. Fuel, food and water allocations remain under the control of the Resilience Command.

Aid groups, economists and a handful of former officials describe an island governing by checklist. The port is open but the world is not: trade has split into rival systems, the straits are patrolled rather than free, and the migrant workforce that built and cleaned the republic has been cut by a third under the strategic labour quota. Johor has hardened its position on the post-2061 water settlement, and the Causeway is a customs border with queues measured in days.

Citizens, for the most part, comply. Whether they consent is a different question, and one the official figures do not measure. Surveillance is dense, protests are rare and the vocabulary of public life has narrowed. A younger generation has left for Sydney, Vancouver and Dublin. Those who remain speak of a protective silence.

street.title: “The circle is permitted because it is useful”
street.text: When the domestic worker quota fell for the third time, Zainab Abdullah, 52, a nurse, helped her block set up a care circle: a rota of neighbours who now look after the oldest residents. It has a registered name, a notebook and a visit from a district officer every other month. “We are permitted because we are useful,” she says, “and watched because we are not official.” Down the corridor, Mr Goh, 88, has lost the helper who cared for him for fourteen years. Maricel, 46, from Cebu, has been told her permit will not be renewed in October. The circle has petitioned for an exception. Mr Goh says nothing. He holds a small flag his late wife sewed. The lift works, the water runs on the ordained hours and the block is quiet. Tonight no one will be on the void deck.

side: Emigration rises for a fifth year
voices: I served to defend the island from the sea. These days I check permits at the reservoir. Nobody asks me whether I am proud.
NSman, 36, posted to critical-zone duty
My daughter's application to Sydney is in, and so is mine. We love this place. We would like it to love us back without checking our phones first.
Dr Koh Wei Ling, 43, paediatrician, Novena
I have cared for Mr Goh for fourteen years. I do not know what happens to him in October. I do not know what happens to me.
Maricel D., 46, domestic worker, Bukit Batok
D.takeaway: This is not collapse. It is a society tolerated for being useful and watched for being unofficial, and the question is how long that holds.

full.pull: We are safe. We are told this often.
full.pullBy: A hospital administrator, speaking off the record

side.p: Twelve more months. A review panel will meet in private, the statement said.
Access to NEWater and desalination plants by permit only.
Registered neighbourhood care circles are filling the gap, and being counted.

side.h: Emigration rises for a fifth year
side.p: One in five citizens aged 25 to 40 now lives abroad, officials estimate.

letters: My son left for Perth on Tuesday. I am relieved and I am hollow. — Reader, Toa Payoh
The water came at 4pm. It was clear. We all noticed. — Reader, Jurong West
Our care circle looked after sixty-two residents last month. Where is the ministry? — Volunteer, Bukit Batok
full.comment: The state has spent the centenary insisting it is in control. In the blocks, people have drawn their own conclusion and, quietly, begun to do for themselves what no department can: look after the very old, share the water hours, settle disputes. This is not collapse. The island is too competent for that. It is something new and uneasy: a society that is tolerated for being useful and watched for being unofficial.
full.extrapolated: Coercion by checklist: not stable fortress and not clean collapse. A narrowed public life, a squeezed non-resident workforce, a hardened Johor and an emigrating middle. If you would pick a different end-state for D, this is the place to say so.
questions: Is coercion by checklist the right end-state? Or should D be a stable fortress (it works) or a failure of consent (it breaks)? We chose the middle: challenge it.
What does the island actually earn in a fragmented world? What keeps the economy alive?
Are citizens consenting, complying or leaving? Be concrete about who can leave and who cannot.
What happens with Malaysia, Indonesia and the straits? Does Johor use water as leverage in 2061?
On the street: who copes, who leaves, and who is left behind, including non-residents?

drift.drifting: Further down and right if the emergency becomes permanent. Upwards if rules begin to replace discretion, or towards A if the blocs thaw and the compact is rebuilt.

Legal space for neighbourhood mutual aid, not just registered tolerance

我女儿申请去悉尼的资料交上去了，我的也是。我们爱这个地方。我们希望它也爱我们，而不必先检查我们的手机。
许薇玲医生，43岁，儿科医生，诺维娜
我照顾吴先生十四年了。我不知道十月之后他会怎样。我也不知道我会怎样。
Maricel D.，46岁，家庭佣工，武吉巴督
today: 每位退休者对应的在职者

A.name: Perkongsian Terbuka
A.line: Kes yang baik: hab yang terus diperlukan dan rakyat yang terus berada di meja.
signals: Keputusan perhimpunan dilaksanakan, bukan sekadar didengar
Pendapatan median warganegara selari dengan KDNK per kapita
Pembangkang dan masyarakat sivil terlibat dalam penelitian bajet
A.headline: Pada usia seratus, sebuah pulau kecil yang belajar berkongsi risikonya
A.dek: Singapura genap seratus tahun dengan Perhimpunan Warganegara, jaminan penjagaan dan perjanjian air yang dimiliki bersama Johor.
A.takeaway: Hab ini bertahan kerana cukup ramai warganegara masih merasakan ia milik mereka. Tugas abad kedua ialah meluaskan bilangan itu sebelum kejutan seterusnya menguji hitungannya.
voices: AI bank mengambil separuh kerja pematuhan saya yang rutin dan kredit negara membawa saya ke separuh yang lain. Pendapatan sejam saya lebih rendah tetapi setahun lebih tinggi, dan malam saya milik saya.
Priya Nair, 44, pakar pematuhan, Bukit Merah
Sewa gerai saya ditetapkan oleh formula yang diundi seluruh jalan. Saya tidak suka formula itu. Saya suka kerana saya membantu menulisnya.
Encik Chew, 58, pemilik kedai kopi, Tiong Bahru
Saya datang dengan permit kerja untuk membina tembok laut. Sebelas tahun kemudian anak perempuan saya warganegara. Saya masih hantar wang ke Kerala, dan saya tidak lagi rasa seperti perabot.
Joseph Mathew, 49, penyelia tapak, penduduk tetap

B.name: Republik Bot Penyelamat
B.line: Dunia berpecah dan pulau ini bersatu: ekonomi lebih kecil dan beban dikongsi.
signals: Formula simpanan diterbitkan dan diaudit
Barisan catuan teratur, aduan didengar
Pekerja bukan pemastautin termasuk dalam formula perkongsian beban
B.headline: Pada usia seratus, sebuah bot penyelamat yang memastikan semua orang kekal di dalamnya
B.dek: Singapura genap seratus tahun dengan ekonomi yang lebih kecil, lebih adil dan lebih berjaga-jaga, dengan formula catuan yang boleh dibaca semua orang.
B.takeaway: Bot penyelamat hanya berfungsi jika tiada siapa disuruh berenang. Soalnya ialah sama ada beban dikongsi mengikut peraturan, atau hanya dalam kalangan warganegara.
voices: Firma saya dahulu menulis polisi untuk empat puluh negara. Kini empat belas, dan kami menulisnya dengan teliti. Pendapatan saya kurang satu pertiga. Cucu saya akan ada kerjaya lebih kecil tetapi meja yang lebih penuh.
Raymond Ong, 61, penanggung insurans marin, Telok Blangah
Saya berkhidmat pada usia lapan belas dan sekali lagi pada lima puluh lapan. Kali kedua saya mengajar remaja membaiki pengubah kuasa. Kedua-dua kali saya rasa berguna.
Gurmit Singh, 59, juruelektrik, Yishun
Jangan panggil ia pengorbanan. Panggillah ia harga sebuah meja yang masih terhidang untuk semua.
Puan Chan, 72, guru bersara, Queenstown

C.name: Hab Bersalut Emas
C.line: Dunia masih mahukan pulau ini. Rakyat pulau ini kurang pasti ia masih mahukan mereka.
signals: Pendapatan median warganegara berbanding KDNK per kapita
Bahagian warganegara dalam jawatan kanan
Dasar tamat pajakan dan penerimaannya
C.headline: Pada usia seratus, sebuah bandar yang diingini seluruh dunia, dan semakin kurang mampu dimiliki penduduknya
C.dek: Modal dan ketibaan rekod, kampus pengiraan dan tembok laut yang siap tepat masa, sementara warganegara menjadi penyewa di bandar sendiri.
C.takeaway: Bandar ini berfungsi. Soalnya untuk siapa ia berfungsi, dan berapa lama teras warganegara akan berpuas hati sebagai penyewa.
voices: Saya tidak pernah berpendapatan setinggi ini atau mempunyai suara sekecil ini tentang tempat tinggal saya. Kedua-duanya boleh benar. Saya tidak mengadu, saya terlalu sibuk.
Anjali Rao, 29, penyelidik keselamatan AI, Pemastautin Global
Ayah saya membina rumah itu. Anak saya akan dihantar sepucuk surat tentangnya.
Encik Tan, 64, juruteknik bersara, Queenstown
Kami tidur lapan orang sebilik di asrama yang ada gimnasium. Saya tidak pernah melihat tembok laut, hanya jalan menuju ke sana.
Rubel Hossain, 31, pekerja binaan, Tuas

D.name: Kota Berkawal
D.line: Kes yang sukar: pulau yang selamat, kehidupan awam yang menyempit dan negara dalam mod pengurusan berpanjangan.
signals: Pembaharuan darurat menjadi rutin
Warganegara berumur 25 hingga 40 berhijrah
Bahagian tenaga kerja bukan pemastautin jatuh kerana kuota, bukan permintaan
D.headline: Pada usia seratus, sebuah pulau yang berjaga-jaga
D.dek: Perbarisan di dalam dewan, Perintah Sumber Darurat pada tahun keempat belas dan kumpulan penjagaan mengisi ruang yang disempitkan negara.
D.takeaway: Ini bukan keruntuhan. Ini masyarakat yang diterima kerana berguna dan diperhatikan kerana tidak rasmi, dan soalnya berapa lama ia bertahan.
voices: Saya berkhidmat untuk mempertahankan pulau ini dari laut. Kini saya memeriksa permit di takungan. Tiada siapa bertanya sama ada saya bangga.
Anggota NS, 36, ditempatkan di zon kritikal
Permohonan anak saya ke Sydney sudah dihantar, begitu juga permohonan saya. Kami sayang tempat ini. Kami mahu ia menyayangi kami kembali tanpa memeriksa telefon kami dahulu.
Dr Koh Wei Ling, 43, pakar pediatrik, Novena
Saya menjaga Encik Goh empat belas tahun. Saya tidak tahu apa jadi kepadanya pada Oktober. Saya tidak tahu apa jadi kepada saya.
Maricel D., 46, pembantu rumah, Bukit Batok
today: Pemotongan berjadual di luar zon keutamaan

A.name: திறந்த பொதுவளம்
A.line: நல்ல நிலை: தேவைப்படும் மையமாகத் தொடர்ந்து இருப்பது, மக்கள் அறையில் தொடர்ந்து இருப்பது.
signals: மன்ற முடிவுகள் கேட்கப்படுவதோடு நிறைவேற்றப்படுகின்றன
குடிமக்களின் நடுநிலை வருமானம் தனிநபர் மொத்த உள்நாட்டு உற்பத்திக்கு ஏற்ப உயர்கிறது
எதிர்க்கட்சிகளும் குடிமைச் சமூகமும் வரவு செலவுத் திட்டச் சோதனையில் பங்கேற்கின்றன
A.headline: நூறாம் ஆண்டில், அபாயங்களைப் பகிரக் கற்ற ஒரு சிறு தீவு
A.dek: குடிமக்கள் மன்றம், பராமரிப்பு உத்தரவாதம், ஜொகூருடன் இணை உரிமை கொண்ட நீர் ஒப்பந்தம் ஆகியவற்றுடன் சிங்கப்பூர் நூறாண்டு காண்கிறது.
A.takeaway: போதுமான குடிமக்கள் இது தங்களுடையது என்று இன்னும் உணர்வதால் இந்த மையம் நிலைத்திருக்கிறது. இரண்டாம் நூற்றாண்டின் பணி, அடுத்த அதிர்ச்சி இந்தக் கணக்கைச் சோதிப்பதற்கு முன் அந்த எண்ணிக்கையை விரிவாக்குவது.
voices: வங்கியின் செயற்கை நுண்ணறிவு என் இணக்கப் பணியின் வழக்கமான பாதியை எடுத்துக்கொண்டது; தேசியக் கடன் என்னை மறுபாதிக்கு அழைத்துச் சென்றது. மணிக்கு குறைவாகவும் ஆண்டுக்கு அதிகமாகவும் சம்பாதிக்கிறேன், என் மாலைகள் எனக்கே சொந்தம்.
பிரியா நாயர், 44, இணக்க நிபுணர், புக்கிட் மேரா
என் கடையின் வாடகை தெருவே வாக்களித்த சூத்திரத்தால் தீர்மானிக்கப்படுகிறது. அந்தச் சூத்திரம் எனக்குப் பிடிக்காது. அதை எழுத நானும் உதவினேன் என்பது பிடிக்கும்.
திரு சியூ, 58, காப்பிக்கடை உரிமையாளர், தியோங் பாரு
கடல் சுவர் கட்ட வேலை அனுமதியில் வந்தேன். பதினொரு ஆண்டுகளுக்குப் பின் என் மகள் குடிமகள். நான் இன்னும் கேரளாவுக்குப் பணம் அனுப்புகிறேன்; இப்போது நான் வீட்டுப் பொருள் போல உணரவில்லை.
ஜோசப் மேத்யூ, 49, கட்டுமானத் தள மேற்பார்வையாளர், நிரந்தரவாசி

B.name: உயிர்காப்புப் படகுக் குடியரசு
B.line: உலகம் பிளவுபடுகிறது, தீவு ஒன்றுசேர்கிறது: சிறிய பொருளாதாரம், பகிரப்படும் சுமை.
signals: இருப்புச் சூத்திரங்கள் வெளியிடப்பட்டுத் தணிக்கை செய்யப்படுகின்றன
ரேஷன் வரிசைகள் ஒழுங்காக உள்ளன, புகார்கள் கேட்கப்படுகின்றன
குடியுரிமையற்ற தொழிலாளர்களும் சுமைப் பகிர்வுச் சூத்திரத்துள் உள்ளனர்
B.headline: நூறாம் ஆண்டில், எல்லோரையும் படகிலேயே வைத்திருந்த உயிர்காப்புப் படகு
B.dek: எல்லோரும் படிக்கக்கூடிய ரேஷன் சூத்திரத்துடன், சிறிய, நியாயமான, விழிப்பான பொருளாதாரத்தில் சிங்கப்பூர் நூறாண்டு காண்கிறது.
B.takeaway: யாரையும் நீந்தச் சொல்லாதபோதுதான் உயிர்காப்புப் படகு பயன்படும். சுமை விதிப்படி பகிரப்படுகிறதா, அல்லது குடிமக்களிடையே மட்டுமா என்பதே கேள்வி.
voices: என் நிறுவனம் நாற்பது நாடுகளுக்குக் காப்பீடு எழுதியது. இப்போது பதினான்குக்கு, கவனமாக எழுதுகிறோம். என் வருமானம் மூன்றில் ஒரு பங்கு குறைவு. என் பேரப்பிள்ளைகளுக்குச் சிறிய தொழில் இருக்கும், ஆனால் நிறைவான உணவுமேசை.
ரேமண்ட் ஓங், 61, கடல்சார் காப்பீட்டாளர், தெலோக் பிளாங்கா
பதினெட்டு வயதில் சேவை செய்தேன், ஐம்பத்தெட்டில் மீண்டும். இரண்டாவது முறை பதின்பருவத்தினருக்கு மின்மாற்றியைப் பழுதுபார்க்கக் கற்றுக்கொடுத்தேன். இரண்டு முறையும் பயனுள்ளவனாக உணர்ந்தேன்.
குர்மித் சிங், 59, மின்பணியாளர், யிஷுன்
அதைத் தியாகம் என்று அழைக்காதீர்கள். எல்லோருக்கும் இன்னும் விரித்து வைக்கப்பட்டுள்ள மேசையின் விலை என்று சொல்லுங்கள்.
திருமதி சான், 72, ஓய்வுபெற்ற ஆசிரியை, குயின்ஸ்டவுன்

C.name: பொன்முலாம் மையம்
C.line: உலகம் இன்னும் இந்தத் தீவை விரும்புகிறது. தீவின் மக்களை அது இன்னும் விரும்புகிறதா என்பது அவர்களுக்கு உறுதியில்லை.
signals: குடிமக்களின் நடுநிலை வருமானமும் தனிநபர் மொத்த உள்நாட்டு உற்பத்தியும்
மூத்த பதவிகளில் குடிமக்களின் பங்கு
குத்தகை முடிவுக் கொள்கையும் அதன் ஏற்பும்
C.headline: நூறாம் ஆண்டில், உலகமே விரும்பும் நகரம், ஆனால் அதன் சொந்த மக்கள் குறைவாகவே தாங்க முடிகிறது
C.dek: சாதனை மூலதனமும் வருகையாளர்களும், கணினி வளாகம், சரியான நேரத்தில் முடிந்த கடல் சுவர்; குடிமக்களோ சொந்த நகரில் வாடகைதாரர்களாகிறார்கள்.
C.takeaway: நகரம் இயங்குகிறது. அது யாருக்காக இயங்குகிறது, குடிமக்கள் மையம் வாடகைதாரர்களாக எவ்வளவு காலம் மனநிறைவுடன் இருக்கும் என்பதே கேள்வி.
voices: இவ்வளவு சம்பாதித்ததில்லை, நான் வாழுமிடம் பற்றிக் குரல் இவ்வளவு குறைவாக இருந்ததுமில்லை. இரண்டும் உண்மையாக இருக்கலாம். நான் புகார் செய்வதில்லை, மிகவும் பிஸி.
அஞ்சலி ராவ், 29, செயற்கை நுண்ணறிவுப் பாதுகாப்பு ஆய்வாளர், உலகளாவிய வாசி
என் தந்தை இந்த வீட்டைக் கட்டினார். என் மகனுக்கு அதைப் பற்றிய கடிதம் அனுப்பப்படும்.
திரு டான், 64, ஓய்வுபெற்ற தொழில்நுட்பர், குயின்ஸ்டவுன்
உடற்பயிற்சிக்கூடம் உள்ள தங்குமிடத்தில் ஓர் அறையில் எட்டுப் பேர் தூங்குகிறோம். நான் கடல் சுவரைப் பார்த்ததில்லை, அதற்குச் செல்லும் சாலையை மட்டும்தான்.
ருபெல் ஹொசைன், 31, கட்டுமானத் தொழிலாளர், துவாஸ்

D.name: காவல் நகரம்
D.line: கடினமான நிலை: பாதுகாப்பான தீவு, சுருங்கிய பொது வாழ்க்கை, நிரந்தர நிர்வாக முறையில் அரசு.
